paragraphs.text: The European Benchmarking Task Force (EBTF), formed by members of the FP7 projects CAESAR, CESAR and DECARBit, produced this report by combining two of its earlier deliverables: the Common Framework Definition Document with assumptions and parameters for carbon capture work, and a set of three technical test cases of power plants with and without CO2 capture. New material on the costs and economics of carbon capture is added. The three reference plants, against which new cycles with innovative capture technologies from the three projects are meant to be benchmarked, are an Advanced Supercritical Pulverized Coal plant, an Integrated Gasification Combined Cycle and a Natural Gas Combined Cycle. Each case is described in general terms and then through its process streams, operational characteristics and operational performance; the last part covers the economics of the three cycles. The report is meant to be usable on its own without the earlier two reports.

This document is the closing deliverable of the European Benchmarking Task Force (EBTF), whose members come from three EC Framework 7 projects. The task force set out to establish a full set of parameters, guidelines and best practices that would serve both these projects and later European R&D work on carbon capture. CAESAR (Carbon-free electricity by Sorption Enhanced Water Gas Shift, SEWGS) applies an optimized SEWGS process to pre-combustion CO2 capture from natural gas and also looks at its use in coal plants; it follows on from CACHET. CESAR (CO2 Enhanced Separation and Recovery) deals with post-combustion capture, and its Work Package 2 addresses integration of all plant elements with capture (boiler, steam generation system, CO2 capture, CO2 compression); it follows on from CASTOR. DECARBIT (Enabling Advanced Pre-combustion Capture Techniques and Plants) targets zero-emission pre-combustion capture plants by 2020 at a capture cost below 15 Euros / ton and the highest feasible capture rate, by working on advanced pre-combustion capture techniques and key enabling technologies.

The EBTF members represent Alstom, E.ON, NTNU, Politecnico di Milano, Shell, TNO, University of Ulster and Vattenfall. The first part of the report gathers parameters intended as a common basis for defining and analysing cycles and comparing technologies, so that comparisons rest on identical fundamental assumptions; the values are not put forward as the correct or best choices for any future plant. Much of the material originates from the FP6 projects ENCAP, DYNAMIS, CASTOR and CACHET. DECARBit contributors are NTNU, Shell, University of Ulster and Alstom; CESAR contributors are TNO, E.ON and Vattenfall; the CAESAR contributor is Politecnico di Milano. The report starts with the unit system and ambient conditions, then specifies three fuels (Bituminous coal, Lignite and Natural Gas), which the authors judge sufficient for power generation technology studies. It then sets parameters for plant modules and processes (air separation, coal gasification, shift reaction, gas turbine, steam cycle and heat exchangers) and finally general items: the efficiency calculation procedure, CO2 treatment and emission limits from solid fuels.

The second part covers three test cases, each with and without CO2 capture, to which new cycles from the three projects should be referred: an Advanced Supercritical Pulverized Coal plant, an Integrated Gasification Combined Cycle and a Natural Gas Combined Cycle. Each case gives a general description, process stream specifications, operational characteristics and performance. All performance figures correspond to nominal base-load operation in "new and clean" condition. The energy penalty of capture is expressed for every case through SPECCA (Specific Primary Energy Consumption for CO2 Avoided).

SPECCA = (HR − HR_REF) / (E_REF − E) = 3600·(1/η − 1/η_REF) / (E_REF − E) (Specific Primary Energy Consumption for CO2 Avoided = extra heat rate per unit of CO2 emission avoided). Here HR is the plant heat rate in kJLHV/kWhel, E is the CO2 emission rate in kgCO2/kWhel, η is the net electrical efficiency, and the subscript REF denotes the same plant without CCS.

The next three chapters were written by CESAR (TNO, Netherlands Organization for Applied Scientific Research, assisted by E.ON and Vattenfall), DECARBIT (NTNU, Norwegian University of Science and Technology, assisted by Alstom, Shell and University of Ulster) and CAESAR (Politecnico di Milano), with Alstom as editor. For benchmarking, the three cases were also recalculated by members of another project (stated as CAESAR, CAESAR and CESAR respectively), so each case includes a comparison of configurations and results from two projects. The cases were discussed in depth within the EBTF and outside opinions were requested on many points, aiming for the document to represent the European carbon capture research community as closely as possible; readers may send comments to any listed author.

The third part sets out criteria and a parameter collection for economic assessment of new technologies and cycles with and without CO2 capture. As for the technical framework, the aim is consistent and reliable comparison on shared assumptions rather than recommending best values, and special care is given to clearly documenting where data and assumptions come from. The final part applies these economic parameters to the three test cases; the ASC, IGCC and NGCC economics chapters were prepared by CESAR (E.ON, Vattenfall and TNO), DECARBIT (University of Ulster, assisted by Shell and Alstom) and CAESAR (Politecnico di Milano) respectively.

The authors stress a caveat on how far the results can be trusted. For two of the cases without capture, the Advanced Super-Critical 800 MW steam plant and the Natural Gas Combined Cycle 834 MWe plant, the calculations match the real performance of many existing state-of-the-art plants, so the net electric efficiency and specific power agree with values achieved by major manufacturers. The Integrated Gasification Combined Cycle 442 MWe case is different: it represents a technology built from the theoretical performance of state-of-the-art components that has not yet been applied at a scale large enough to validate the figures. The same lack of validating plants applies to all three capture cases, since only small pilot plants exist so far. Confidence in the results therefore differs strongly between cases, and this reservation applies to the technical results and even more to the economic ones.

This section fixes the most basic definitions: the unit system for formal technology comparisons and economic evaluations, and the ambient conditions used in calculations. 2.1.1 Units: SI units (Système International d'Unités) are to be used in all reports and presentations. 2.1.2 Ambient conditions: although real conditions are site-specific, ISO standard conditions for an inland site with natural draught cooling towers were chosen. 2.1.2.1 Air: pressure 0.101325 MPa, temperature 15 oC, relative humidity 60%, composition as given in the air composition table.

Another temperature may be used if the effect of that choice is made clear.

This section gives guidance for gas turbine performance calculations. The reference machine type is a large-scale "F class" 50 Hz gas turbine, whose 2008-9 state-of-the-art performance, taken from manufacturer data published in Gas Turbine World – 2008 Performance Specifications, is summarized in Table 2.6.1. The data assume ISO-condition air at the compressor inlet and natural gas fuel.

Table 2.6.1 – Plant output, net plant efficiency, pressure ratio, turbine outlet temperature and specific work of large-scale gas turbines of the "F class". Alstom GT-26 (GT with sequential combustion): Plant Output=289.1 MW; Net Plant Efficiency=39.1 %; Pressure Ratio=33.4; Turbine Outlet Temperature=615 °C; Specific Work=451 kJ/kg. GE 9371F: Plant Output=279.2 MW; Net Plant Efficiency=37.9 %; Pressure Ratio=18.3; Turbine Outlet Temperature=630 °C; Specific Work=426 kJ/kg. Siemens STG5-4000F: Plant Output=286.6 MW; Net Plant Efficiency=39.5 %; Pressure Ratio=17.9; Turbine Outlet Temperature=577 °C; Specific Work=416 kJ/kg.

For the two models without sequential combustion (GE 9371F and Siemens STG5-4000F), net output, specific work and net efficiency fall within 280-285 MW, 416-426 kJ/kg and 38-39%, while pressure ratio ranges over 17.9-18.3 and TOT over 577-630°C. On this basis a "reference, average" large F-class gas turbine is defined by: pressure ratio 18.1; inlet filter pressure drop dp = 0.001 MPa; exhaust pressure drop dp = 0.001 MPa (no HRSG); natural gas pressure at the combustor inlet 2.31 MPa, i.e. 5 bar above compressor outlet pressure; net efficiency= 38.5%; specific work = 420 kJ/kg, where specific work is gas turbine output divided by compressor intake mass flow; Turbine Outlet Temperature (TOT) = 603 °C.

Many different gas turbine performance models are in use, so no particular computational method is prescribed. Turbine cooling, for instance, is handled in various ways, and compressor and turbine may be computed stage by stage, from maps or with lumped models. For use in CO2 capture cycles, a model must properly handle changed working conditions and fuel properties. Because different cooled-expansion models give different temperatures and cooling flows, the values used to calibrate TIT should be reported together with the cooling flows. TIT (turbine inlet temperature) is defined as the mixed temperature of the combustor exit flow and all cooling flows, and cooling flow is the cooling air mass flow divided by the compressor intake mass flow. A full mass and energy balance including thermodynamic states of the main streams should be supplied.

Many capture approaches change gas turbine operating conditions, sometimes with large performance effects, for example a different working fluid composition (oxy-combustion cycles) or a fuel with much lower volumetric heating value (the H2-rich fuel of an IGCC with capture). When the cycle differs from the air/NG gas turbine, the following is recommended. (1) Validate the model so that it reproduces the reference average performance (specific work, net plant efficiency, turbine outlet temperature) at the stated conditions: ISO conditions, the given pressure ratio and pressure drops, air as working fluid and the reference natural gas fuel. (2) Document the method used to predict performance under conditions far from the air/methane machine, which may cover: (a) general shifts in compressor and turbine efficiency due to fluid properties, number of stages and blade geometry; (b) the choked nozzle equations linking pressure, temperature and flow at turbine inlet, for evaluating given/existing machines; (c) lowering or raising turbine inlet temperature because of higher or lower heat transfer flux, e.g. with more H2O; (d) adjusting cooling flow so that blade maximum metal temperature stays as with air/NG. (3) Supply the new, modified mass and energy balance with thermodynamic states at the key points.

2.7.1 Cycle configuration: PC-boiler steam cycles are the world's preferred route for coal power, giving high availability and the lowest electricity cost. Ultra-supercritical live steam conditions of 300 bar, 600/610 oC are chosen to match current large plants, and the water pre-heaters deliver boiler feed-water at 315 oC. 2.7.2 Fired boilers, basic parameters for Bituminous coal: one pressure level; boiler exit 300 bar, 600 oC; single reheat at 60 bar, 620 oC; boiler efficiency 95%. Pressure losses: ∆p cold = 3% per heat exchanger; ∆p reheat,cold = 10%; ∆p steam_pipe+valve = 7%. Temperature loss from superheater / reheater to turbine: 2 oC. Natural circulation is assumed.

2.7.3 Heat Recovery Steam Generator - HRSG. Basic parameters: triple pressure with single reheat; reheat is done by mixing superheated IP steam with cold reheat steam before the reheater; η HRSG = 99.7%. Pressure losses: ∆p HRSG-hot = 3 kPa; ∆p HRSG-cold = 3% per heat exchanger; ∆p reheat-cold,tot = 10%; ∆p steam-pipe,valve: HP 7%, IP 9%, IP 9% for reheat IP steam mixing, LP 12%. Temperature loss from superheater / reheater to turbine: 1kJ/kg (approximately 0.5 K). Temperature differences: ∆T steam-gas = 25 oC; ∆T pinch point gas-boiling liquid = 10 oC; ∆T gas-liquid = 10 oC; ∆ approach-ECO = 5 oC. Natural circulation is assumed.

2.7.4 Condenser: a water-cooled steam condenser with a natural draft cooling tower; condenser pressure 0.0048 MPa at a saturation temperature printed as 26. oC in the source (digit after the decimal point missing); cooling water pumping work 0.5% of steam turbine power; cooling water pressure 0.2 - 0.25 MPa; the condensate leaving the condenser is taken as saturated. 2.7.5 Steam turbines, isentropic efficiencies: η HP = 92%; η IP = 94%; η LP = 88% including leaving losses. Steam extraction pressure losses: HP extraction pipe + preheater 3%; LP extraction pipe + preheater 5%. 2.7.6 Pumps: efficiency 70%.

These rules cover heat exchangers outside the steam cycle. 2.8.1 Pinch points: gas / gas 25 oC; gas / boiling or liquid phase 10 oC; liquid / liquid 10 oC; condensing / liquid 3 oC. They are reference guidance only; metallurgy, size, pressure or composition can affect heat transfer and very small temperature differences may sometimes be suitable, so other justified values are allowed. 2.8.2 Pressure drop: pressure drop depends strongly on phase, and liquid-side drop is normally an absolute value independent of pressure level; nevertheless, for simplicity and given the endless range of cases, a relative approach is used for liquids too. Liquid phase pressure drop, cold and hot side: 0.04 MPa; gas phase pressure drop, cold and hot side: 2%.

2.9.1 Specific values: mechanical efficiency η m = 99.6%; generator efficiency η G = 98.5%; auxiliary power η Aux is estimated case by case. 2.9.2 Power island: the power island efficiency is to be computed with the formula below. η_net,PI = [(W_T + W_C)·η_m·η_g + W_ST·η_m·η_g + W_P + W_aux] / (ṁ_f·LHV) (net power island efficiency = gas turbine and steam turbine net shaft work after mechanical and generator losses, minus pump and auxiliary consumption, divided by fuel heat input). Symbols: η_net,PI net efficiency of the Power Island (-); ṁ_f fuel flow rate (kg/s); LHV lower heating value (kJ/kg); W_T turbine work from fluid enthalpy change (kW, >0); W_C compressor work from fluid enthalpy change (kW, <0); η_m mechanical efficiency (-); η_g generator efficiency (-); W_ST steam turbine work from fluid enthalpy change (kW, >0); W_P total pump work including feed water and cooling water pumps (kW, <0); W_aux,PI total auxiliary work of the power island only (kW, <0).

2.10.3 Compression: the final pressure is 11 MPa, and the compressed CO2 is cooled to the cooling water temperature of an inland site at 15°C and 60% humidity (ISO conditions, Section 2.1) plus a suitable pinch, i.e. below 30°C. The procedure described here is one option; other efficiencies or intercooler counts may be used if clearly stated. The compression energy is pre-estimated so that net efficiency can be obtained without simulating compression: from 0.15 MPa to 11.0 MPa the total electricity need is put at 0.34 MJ/kg CO2 (wet base). This figure comes from an example calculation; other justified values are acceptable, and impurity content, for example, can change the requirement.

Compression up to 8.0 MPa uses three intercooled compressor stages with discharge pressures of 0.435 MPa (stage 1), 1.865 MPa (stage 2) and 8.0 MPa (stage 3), and polytropic efficiencies of 80%, 80% and 75% respectively. Compressor driver efficiency is 95%. Dense-phase CO2 is then pumped from 8.0 MPa to the final pressure with 75% pump efficiency and 95 % driver efficiency. paragraphs.section: 3.1 Introduction to the ASC Test Case
paragraphs.text: This chapter sets out the baseline solvent-based post-combustion CO2 capture process applied to an Advanced SuperCritical (ASC) pulverized fuel (PF) power plant firing bituminous coal. It is one of three test plants (two solid-fuel, one natural gas) defined in CESAR for evaluating post-combustion capture. The solvent is a 30% (by weight) aqueous monoethanolamine (MEA) solution. The capture process was modelled in ASPEN Plus with a baseline CO2 removal of 90%, and the model results were used to design and size the equipment, which in turn underpins the capital and operating cost estimates of the capture plant. Power plant performance and the integration of capture and power plant were evaluated jointly by Doosan Babcock, E.ON and Siemens, so the case reflects input from Doosan Babcock, Siemens, E.ON and TNO (capture design).

3.2.1 Case Description and Flow Diagram: an Advanced SuperCritical (ASC) boiler and turbine produce 819 MWe(gross) without capture; after auxiliary consumption the net output is 754.3MWe, giving a net cycle efficiency of 45.5%. The layout assumes an inland site with natural draft cooling towers and coal delivered by rail, with site conditions (ambient and cooling water temperatures, etc.), coal properties and equipment efficiencies taken from the EBTF Common Framework Definition Document. Figure 3.2.1 gives the block flow diagram of the 800MWe supercritical plant; the power block comprises the steam turbine, the steam generator with coal bunker bay, and the central switch gear. 3.2.1.1 Steam Turbine Plant: HP, IP and LP turbines with extraction points for regenerative heating of condensate and feed water, using nine feed water heaters; the condensers sit beneath the LP turbines, and motor driven boiler feed pumps are chosen for base-load duty following supplier advice.

3.2.1.2 Steam Generator Plant: a state-of-the-art Doosan Babcock Two-Pass single reheat BENSON boiler with a Low Mass Flux Vertical Internally Ribbed Tube (LMVT) Furnace is used to maximize performance, and a start-up and low load operation system protects the furnace. 3.2.1.3 Power Plant Auxiliaries: coal milling uses 6 vertical spindle, ring and roller slow speed pressurized mills with seal air fans. Combustion uses 30 Doosan Babcock Low NOx Axial Swirl burners plus in-furnace air-staging (BOFA) as primary NOx control. Combustion air and flue gas systems operate in balanced draught with two trains, and separate primary and secondary regenerative air heaters warm the combustion air and enable coal drying and pulverized fuel transport. Emission control comprises a selective catalytic reduction (SCR) DeNOx plant between boiler exit and air heater inlet, electrostatic precipitators and a wet limestone desulphurization plant ahead of the flue stack. Fly ash is handled by a dry conveying system and furnace bottom ash by continuous removal with a submerged chain conveyer.

3.3.1 Case Description and Flow Diagram: the central step of post-combustion capture is separating CO2 from flue gas, which can be done by absorption, adsorption, membranes or other physical and biological routes. Here a conventional amine scrubbing process is applied: a basic absorption-desorption scheme with 30% wt MEA solvent, regarded as the benchmark technology and already used in several industrial applications. The case is a new plant designed for capture operation over its whole lifetime, with 90% of the flue gas CO2 captured and full load operation considered. Including planned and forced outages, the annual average load factor is 85%. Capture plant inlet flue gas conditions (equal to FGD outlet) are in Table 3.3.1.1; Fig. 3.3.1.1 is the block diagram of the plant with capture and Fig. 3.3.1.2 the detailed capture flow sheet used to assess capture requirements.

The flue gas is first cooled to 50ºC and then enters the absorber, where it contacts the MEA solvent. State-of-the-art FGD brings SO2 down to 85 mg/Nm3 (about 30ppm), and an additional washing step could lower it further; whether to include it depends on a careful assessment of solvent degradation and cost. In this case, MEA loss through irreversible reaction with SO2 is accounted for in the economic evaluation using estimates from Rubin and Rao, 2002. Under absorber conditions CO2 is chemically bound to MEA, according to the reactions in Table 3.3.1.2. A blower drives the gas through the absorber, after which it passes a water wash section that balances system water and captures entrained solvent droplets or vapour before leaving.

The CO2-rich solvent is pumped through a heat exchanger to the stripper top. Regeneration happens in the stripper at about 120ºC and slightly above atmospheric pressure, with a reboiler supplying heat to warm the solvent, produce stripping vapour and provide the desorption heat for releasing bound CO2; this imposes a large thermal penalty on the host plant. The steam can be taken from the steam turbine IP/LP crossover, which is at 5.2 bar in the plant without capture. The reboiler needs 3 bara steam, a 0.5 bar drop is assumed between crossover and reboiler, and the crossover pressure must stay at least 3.5 bara.

Because extracting steam from the crossover of the base design would drop its pressure below 3.5 bara, the LP turbines were redesigned for the capture case to hold 3.5 bara at full load. The extracted steam is conditioned by pressure reduction and attemperation before the reboiler; attemperation uses reboiler condensate to desuperheat the steam, which reduces the extraction flow and so the MEA efficiency penalty on the steam cycle. Reboiler inlet steam is at 134ºC and 3.05 bar, and the condensate returns to the boiler feed water train. Stripping steam is condensed and refluxed to the stripper while the CO2 product leaves the condenser; after most residual water is removed the CO2 is relatively pure (> 99%), mostly with water vapour as remaining component. The lean solvent, still holding some CO2, returns to the absorber after passing the lean-rich heat exchanger and then a cooler that lowers it to absorber temperature.

4.3.3.1 Shift Reactors: shifting converts the carbon species in the syngas into CO2, which can then be removed by physical absorption, while generating extra H2. A "sour shift" ("dirty shift") of CO in the raw gas is performed over two catalytic beds at 300 °C and 250 °C. A steam to CO ratio of 1.9 in the first reactor gives roughly 96% CO conversion, and each bed has a 1 bar pressure drop. H2S goes to the Claus plant with flue gas recycle, and CO2 is then captured from the sulphur free syngas.

The Selexol solvent is regenerated by flashing at 5, 2.3 and 1.05 bar and returned to absorption; the CO2 is compressed to 110 bar and piped to storage. CO2 capture requires solvent refrigeration to 5°C, whereas for H2S the solvent is regenerated with steam heating to about 150 °C. paragraphs.section: 5.1 Introduction to the NGCC Test Case
paragraphs.text: This chapter sets the natural gas power test case. The configuration, proposed by CAESAR, is one possible arrangement for a gas-fired plant. Two reference plants, without and with capture, are defined to quantify the efficiency, output and cost penalties of carbon capture, and the technology reflects current state-of-the-art large base-load plants without capture. For the capture plant, a NGCC with post-combustion chemical absorption using MEA sorbent is chosen, because it integrates more simply with the power cycle (the gas turbine is unchanged) and is more reliable than other routes such as pre-combustion decarbonisation.

paragraphs.section: 5.1 Introduction to the NGCC Test Case
paragraphs.text: The approach was to (i) pick large base-load plants representative of the state of the art, (ii) compute power output, efficiency and specific emissions for each under one consistent and complete set of assumptions, and (iii) report detailed results, including energy and mass balances, for use as a reference in future simulations. All calculations used the code GS of the Department of Energy of the Politecnico di Milano, which can produce detailed energy and mass balances for an almost unlimited range of plant schemes; the same code is applied to all innovative CAESAR schemes so that the proposals are compared consistently.

5.2.1 Case description and flow diagram: the reference NGCC without capture has two identical large-scale "F class" gas turbines based on the generic EBTF Common Framework model, each with its own heat recovery steam generator (HRSG), and both HRSGs feed one steam turbine. The HRSG has three pressure levels + reheat. Natural gas is preheated to 160°C with feed-water drawn from the IP drum before entering the combustor, improving plant efficiency, and the combustor fuel rate is set so that TIT equals the case without fuel preheating. 5.3.1 Case description and flow diagram: capture is by chemical absorption of CO2 into MEA. The absorption column operates at 1.1 bar, with a booster fan ahead of it to overcome pressure drops so that the GT exhaust pressure matches that of a conventional NGCC without capture. CO2 absorbed by MEA is released in the stripper, which needs heat for amine regeneration; this comes from steam extracted from the steam turbine and de-superheated with LP saturated water. The released CO2 is compressed in an inter-cooled compressor, liquefied at 80 bar and pumped to the 110 bar delivery pressure. Fig. 5.3.1.1 – Simplified flow diagram of the NGCC case with capture. The capture simulation gives a regeneration energy of 3.95 GJ/tonnCO2. MEA regeneration heat is supplied by 4.0 bar steam, roughly 1.85 kg of steam per kg of CO2 captured, bled at the IP-LP cross-over and saturated with LP drum water.

Exhaust gas is cooled downstream of the HRSG to the 40°C needed at the absorber. The absorber and stripper are modelled with 3 and 10 vapour-liquid equilibrium stages respectively. In the model the MEA loop is opened, with a splitter and make-up on the stripper-to-absorber stream, only to save computing time; in a real plant the solvent loop is closed and fresh MEA is only added to offset degradation, which is not simulated. Whether the proposed CO2 capture cycles are worthwhile depends not only on good technical performance but strongly on their overall economics. The assessment runs in stages: first a common set of assumptions is fixed so that cycles can be judged consistently; next the base case plants with and without capture are costed, and all novel cycles are compared with these references. Its core elements are estimates of investment, of fixed and variable operation and maintenance costs and of fuel costs, plus calculation of breakeven electricity selling prices. The same method is to be used for the novel systems, with the added step of costing new components and their influence on overall financial performance. Economic viability is judged primarily by CO2 avoidance cost and breakeven electricity selling price, while indirectly related aspects such as cycling behaviour, reliability and flexibility should also be discussed, and sensitivity analyses reveal the influence of the most volatile parameters.

The chapter lists the assumptions for assessing the economics of novel technologies, from which lifetime costs can be derived. Total capital cost is estimated either with a Bottom Up Approach (BUA), i.e. the step-count exponential costing method based on dominant or combined parameters from the mass and energy balance, or with a Top Down Approach (TDA) using supplier estimates of the whole EPC (Engineering, Procurement and Construction) cost. Fixed and variable O&M and fuel costs are derived from material, fuel and energy flows together with the specified values. A net present value calculation then gives the breakeven electricity selling prices, and because some assumptions are uncertain, a series of sensitivity analyses forms part of the impact assessment.

Economic boundary conditions cover the main plant life cycle assumptions from construction to decommissioning. The reference year for all assessments is 2008, when the three EBTF projects began. Because economic swings in that period make like-for-like costing difficult, an average Chemical Engineering Plant Cost Index (CEPCI) of 576% is assumed for 2008 (1958 = 100%, see Fig. 6.2). Proposals to use 2015 or 2020, when the technology might be available, were turned down since long-term economic trends are hard to forecast. The assumed average exchange rate for the period is €0.683/$ (€1.258/£). Fig. 6.2 – Chemical Engineering Plant Cost Index (monthly 2004-2010).

The economic plant lifetime is 25 years, although economics could improve considerably if components such as the gas turbine outlast their design life. Sensitivity runs are recommended with, for example, 40 years for coal plants (a typical lifetime used in ENCAP, CASTOR and CESAR) and 15 years for natural gas plants. Membrane lifetime defaults to eight years with a ±50% range unless stated otherwise, so the sensitivity range is 4 to 12 years. Construction including commissioning is assumed to take four years for coal and lignite plants and 3 years for natural gas cycles, with yearly spending shares as in Table 6.2.

Table 6.2 – Annual allocation of finances for plant construction. Year 1: Allocation 3 years=40%; Allocation 4 years=20%. Year 2: Allocation 3 years=30%; Allocation 4 years=30%. Year 3: Allocation 3 years=30%; Allocation 4 years=30%. Year 4: Allocation 3 years=0; Allocation 4 years=20%.

The financial analysis uses a real (inflation-free) average discounted cash flow rate (DCF) of eight percent, a hurdle rate representing an average cost of capital that accounts for required equity returns and loan interest. To cover future uncertainty the DCF is varied by ±50% in sensitivity analysis (DCF: 4-12%). Since corporate and emission taxes differ widely between member states and change over the project life, all cycle economics are on a pre-taxation basis, and depreciation is likewise left out.

Total Engineering, Procurement and Construction (EPC) cost is computed by two approaches. (1) The Bottom Up Approach (BUA) is used for the post-combustion CO2 capture and compression processes of CESAR and CAESAR and for all IGCC and NGCC concepts with and without capture from DECARBIT and CAESAR. Its steps are: (a) Module/Equipment Costs, estimating each main equipment module with the step-count exponential method from dominant or combined mass and energy balance parameters plus supplier or other cost data, their sum being the Total Equipment Cost (TEC); (b) Installation costs, added for integrating modules into the plant, such as piping/valves, civil works, instrumentation, electrical installations, insulation, painting, steel structures, erection and OSBL (outside battery limits); (c) Total Direct Plant Cost (TDPC), the sum of equipment and installation costs; (d) Indirect Costs, fixed at 14% of the TDPC for every technology and covering yard improvement, service facilities, engineering, buildings and sundries (breakdown in Table 6.4).
Table 6.4 – Breakdown of Indirect costs (% of TDPC). Yard improvement=1.5%; Service facilities=2%; Engineering/consultancy cost=4.5%; Building=4%; Miscellaneous=2%.

Remaining BUA steps: (e) EPC is TDPC plus Indirect Costs; (f) Owner's Costs and Contingencies, covering owner planning, design, commissioning and working capital plus contingencies, set at 15% of total EPC for all technologies; (g) Total Plant Cost (TPC), equal to EPC plus owner's costs and contingencies. (2) The Top Down Approach (TDA) is applied in CESAR to the ASCPF (Advanced Super-Critical Pulverized Fuel boiler) and NGCC base plants, with EPC taken directly from supplier estimates for the whole plant; DECARBIT also costed the ASCPF base plant by BUA to compare the two approaches. Owner's costs and contingencies are again 15% of EPC and TPC is EPC plus these. All capital costs are expressed at 2008 price level, and development and land costs are excluded.

The cycles are designed for base load, but experience shows that unforeseen technical problems in early years mean capacity factor must be ramped up gradually: about 40% in the first year and 65% in the second after construction, and more than 85% from the third year on. Mine-mouth coal prices have been steady recently, but market prices have climbed substantially. Bituminous coal is priced at €3/GJ and lignite at €1.2/GJ, with sensitivity of -50% to + 50% (€1.5/GJ-€4.5/GJ for bituminous coal and 0.6-1.7 for lignite). Natural gas is €6.5/GJ, varied between €4/GJ and €9/GJ. DECARBit has no natural gas fired cycles, yet a small natural gas consumption should be included for start-up and cycling.

Table 6.5 – Cost of main consumables. Clean water: Cost=€6/m3 (range €4 m3 -€8 m3). Cooling water: Cost=€0.35 /m3. Ash disposal: Cost=€0-32/t (zero cost if the ash can be used in construction or mining). Limestone: Cost=€36/t (€24-48/t).

Two indicators are used as the main measures of a cycle's economic performance, the breakeven electricity selling price (BESP) and the CO2 avoidance cost; BESP incorporates the plant's total capital cost and all O&M costs. Sensitivity analysis should show how volatile variables affect BESP and CO2 avoidance cost, the key ones being specific investment, discounted cash flow rate, fuel price, capacity factor and operating and maintenance cost.

paragraphs.section: 8.1 Introduction to the IGCC economic test case
paragraphs.text: This chapter examines the economics of the integrated gasification combined cycles (IGCC) described in Section 4, drawing on test cases and early benchmarking results from the three projects. The first case is a conventional plant without CO2 capture producing 391.45 MW net; the second includes a CO2 capture plant and produces 352.74MW net. The techno-economic analysis uses the ECLIPSE chemical plant simulation package, first built for European Commission power plant research such as the Joule II programme (R&D in Clean Coal Technology) and since applied to many chemical and engineering processes, with validation through numerous real process simulations over the years.

At present IGCC capital cost may exceed that of established systems by over 30 percent because of foreseen or unforeseen events such as construction delays, larger liquidated damage requirements and new component development, so the sensitivity analysis spans ±30 percent investment. Early plants may need public support to be viable; most US IGCC power projects received government incentives, mainly capital to buy down equipment cost. Costs are expected to fall to a steady level as experience accumulates, following a logistic decay model.

dI/dN = k·I·((M − I)/M) (1) (rate of change of investment per additional plant built follows logistic decay). I = Investment; M = Maximum cost, i.e. the cost of the first plants; k = constant setting the descent and shape of the change; N = number of IGCC plants built.

Since large IGCC plants have no track record, the equilibrium investment level is hard to predict; for the reasoning here it is taken equal to the current investment level of conventional coal plants, with the investment band set per sections 2 and 6. Solution: I = E + (M − E)/(1 + C·e^(Nk)) = M/(1 + r) + [M(1 + r) − M] / [(1 + C·e^(Nk))(1 + r)] (2) (capital investment of the nth plant decays from the first-of-a-kind cost toward the equilibrium target). I = capital investment of the nth plant; M = maximum capital investment; E = investment target once cost equilibrium is reached; r = additional cost of first-of-a-kind plants in percentage; C = scaling factor.

Figure 8.4 shows possible cost development curves for the IGCC case without capture for various k constants and starting values: a high k means rapid technical development and market uptake, a low k slow progress. The scaling factor C is 0.01 in this example, and a negative C would mean rising cost. C, k and E can change stepwise with market conditions. Plant cost indices, location factors and inflation are not in the equation but can be captured through C and k, and plants from different years or locations must be normalised accordingly. Van den Broek used a similar method, with scenarios based on single learning curve models with an experience factor describing IGCC cost development to 2050. Fig. 8.4 - Conventional IGCC cost development scenarios.

Many routes exist to lower total capital investment. Literature highlights techno-economic optimisation of a) air separation units, b) gas turbine operation and c) syngas processing and cleaning (warm versus cold gas clean up). Feedstock variability, better flexibility and availability, multi-product schemes and adaptation to other industrial processes are equally relevant, and novel technologies to improve IGCC techno-economics are being studied worldwide, alongside R&D on alternative generation technologies such as the NETL project (DOE/NETL-2009/1361) on integrated coal gasification fuel cells. In Shell-based IGCC with capture the energy penalty lies more in fuel gas processing, whereas other options lose much internal energy to oxygen production and/or CO2 separation, purification and compression. The study finds that Shell-based IGCC needs further energy gains and performance optimisation to become a preferred future option; the emerging DECARBit cycles are key to this, and better performance will necessarily improve the economics.

As usual for gas-fired cycles, natural gas cost dominates at about 250 M€/y, i.e. 75% of COE without capture; with capture, higher investment and extra operating costs lower this share to 67%. The capture case has a COE of 69.3 €/MWh, 30% above the reference, and a cost of CO2 avoided of about 48 €/tCO2. Relative to the CESAR layout with 1 gas turbine and 1 steam turbine, the CAESAR configuration with 2 gas turbines and 1 steam turbine saves about 20% of investment cost through scale effects. paragraphs.section: 9.6 Breakeven electricity selling price and sensitivity analysis
paragraphs.text: NGCC BESP with and without capture is determined from net present value (NPV) calculations, giving typical values of €54.14/MWh without capture and €69.14/MWh with capture. Capacity factor is 65% in the first year and 85% afterwards, since start-up is easier for NGCC than for coal plants; whether the improved economics justify extra maintenance and overhaul cost still needs checking. Fig. 9.6.1 a-e shows how investment cost (a), fuel price (b), operating cost (c), capacity factor (d) and efficiency loss (e) affect BESP without capture; the fuel price assumption reflects 2008 trends that turned out to be short lived.

paragraphs.section: 9.6 Breakeven electricity selling price and sensitivity analysis
paragraphs.text: Figure 9.6.2 gives the sensitivity for the capture case (NGCC/CO2), which needs over 30% more capital and 100% more operating cost at nearly 9 percent point lower efficiency, raising BESP by 15 €/MWh, i.e. 30%. Figure 9.6.3 shows NGCC/CO2 avoidance cost under ±30 % specific investment variation: the default is €47.6/t at a discounted cash flow (DCF) of 8% with the specific investment of Table 9.5.2, using a specific emission of 36 kg/MWh versus 352 kg/MWh for the conventional NGCC.

paragraphs.section: 9.6 Breakeven electricity selling price and sensitivity analysis
paragraphs.text: Fig. 9.6.1 - Sensitivity analysis for the test case without CO2 capture, panels a) BESP versus SI, b) BESP versus fuel price, c) BESP versus operating cost variations, d) BESP versus capacity factor, e) BESP versus efficiency loss, for DCF 4%, DCF 8% and DCF 12% (SI: specific investment without contingency and owner's cost). Figure 9.6.2 - The same sensitivity panels for the test case with CO2 Capture. Figure 9.6.3 - CO2 avoidance cost of NGCC/CO2 versus SI variation (Min, Default, Max; 4%, 8% and 12% DCF).

Chapters 3, 4 and 5 presented the technical analysis of the three test cases, each performed by two of the projects CAESAR, CESAR and DECARBit, and chapters 7, 8 and 9 their economics; tables 10.1 to 10.3 summarize the results. Overall agreement between projects is very good given that different teams used different computer codes and often different process and equipment models, and the efficiencies in particular match remarkably well. The European Benchmarking Task Force thus met its goal of showing that different teams with different tools reach similar results from a similar set of assumptions and parameters, which is mainly given in Sections 2 and 6, with a few further assumptions stated in other sections. For the ASC case, the near-identical assumptions of the two projects led to practically equal gross electricity production, efficiencies and no-capture emissions; Table 10.1 also includes the Section 7 economic results.

The results allow teams in current and future projects to assess their own technology proposals consistently and with good justification, using the assumption and parameter sets of Sections 2 and 6, so that the advantages or drawbacks of one technology relative to another can be shown credibly to a good approximation.
